title: Date Normalizer & Extractor
description: Multi-format parse — scan text for ISO, US-slash, and long-month dates with `matchAll`, normalize each to `YYYY-MM-DD`, dedupe via a Set, and sort (ISO strings sort lexicographically = chronologically).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the formats and the output contract.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I get a free-text string — a medical or legal note — and I need to extract every calendar date, normalize them to ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`, dedupe, and return them sorted ascending. Clarifying questions:"

• What date formats are in scope? I'd assume ISO `2024-01-05`, US-slash `01/05/2024` (MM/DD/YYYY), and long-month `Jan 5, 2024` / `January 5, 2024`. Anything else — European DD/MM/YYYY, dotted `2024.01.05`, written-out `5th of January`?
• Ambiguous formats — `02/03/2024` is Feb 3 (US) or March 2 (EU). If both could be in the data, I'd need a locale hint or I'd reject ambiguous ones.
• Two-digit years — `01/05/24`? Reject as ambiguous (1924 vs 2024) or windowed (50–99 → 19xx, else 20xx)?
• Validation depth — do I check that month is 1–12 and day is valid for the month, or just structural? (`2024-13-45` could parse and pass through.)
• Duplicate handling — if the same calendar date appears in two formats, return one entry. Confirmed expectation.
sections.why: The DD/MM/YYYY ambiguity question is the one that matters for real data — most US codebases assume MM/DD and silently mangle European inputs, or vice versa. Calling it out upfront either gets you a 'US format only' confirmation (which collapses the problem) or surfaces the harder version. The validation-depth question is the senior-tier one: most candidates parse and trust; flagging that `2024-13-45` should probably be rejected shows you've handled medical-record data before.

sections.title: 2. Spot the shape
sections.prompt: What's the structural pattern — and why a Set, not an array?
sections.say:
"This is text-scan + normalize + dedupe. Three pieces:"

• **Scan**: one regex per format with `String.matchAll(/.../g)` so I get capture groups for year/month/day. `match(/.../g)` would throw the groups away.
• **Normalize**: every match becomes ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`. Zero-pad month and day with `String(n).padStart(2, '0')` so single-digit months from MM/DD or `Jan 5` widen to two digits.
• **Dedupe**: a `Set<string>` of normalized values. The same calendar date written in two formats — `'Jan 5, 2024'` and `'2024-01-05'` — collapses to a single entry because they normalize to the same canonical string.

"And the closer: ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` is designed so plain lexicographic string sort equals chronological order. No `new Date()`, no comparator, no locale issues — just `[...found].sort()`. The fixed-width zero-padded year-first format does the work for me."
sections.why: Naming 'Set keyed on normalized form, not raw match' is the load-bearing insight — it's what makes dedupe automatic. The alternative — keep raw strings, then dedupe at the end — requires comparing across formats and is much harder. The ISO-sort-equals-chronological-sort point is the elegance argument: the format choice eliminates an entire layer of comparison logic. Saying it out loud shows you understand WHY ISO is the canonical normalized form, not just that it is.

sections.title: 3. Walk a tiny example
sections.prompt: Trace one input end-to-end to confirm the model.
sections.intro: "Let me run a one-sentence note through the three regex passes."

examples.note: Three matches across three formats — but two of them are the same calendar day, so Set dedupes them.

sections.why: The dedupe step is what makes this case interesting — without the Set, the output would be `['2024-01-05', '2024-02-10', '2024-01-05']` and a caller would think the patient was seen twice on Jan 5. Tracing it makes the Set's job concrete: it's not 'avoid double-counting' in the abstract, it's 'collapse two source spellings into one calendar entry'. The pad-when-normalizing detail (the `Jan 5` case) also matters — without padPath you'd get `'2024-1-5'` and the dedupe would fail because the strings wouldn't match.

sections.title: 4. Edge cases & failure modes
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• **Malformed dates that match structurally** — `2024-13-45` matches the ISO regex perfectly but isn't a real date. We don't validate ranges here; if downstream code does date arithmetic it'll discover the bug. Worth calling out as a known limitation.
• **Embedded false positives** — `pages 1/2/2024 through 3/4/2024` would match the slash regex even though it's a page range. The `\b` word boundaries help, but contextual false positives are unavoidable without NLP. Accept that scan precision tops out around 95%.
• **Month abbreviations with periods** — `Jan.`, `Feb.`, `Sept.`. The regex allows an optional `\.?` after the word, so `Jan. 5, 2024` matches. But `Septem` (a partial typo) would also match `[A-Za-z]+` and then `months['septem']` would be undefined — the `if (mo)` guard skips it. The guard earns its keep.
• **Case sensitivity in month names** — `JANUARY 5, 2024` should work. We lowercase before the months-table lookup; the regex `[A-Za-z]+` already accepts any case.
• **Single-digit days/months without padding** — `Jan 5, 2024` gives `m[2]='5'`. Without `pad(+m[2])` we'd get `'2024-01-5'` which (a) doesn't dedupe against `'2024-01-05'` and (b) doesn't sort right. The pad is mandatory, not cosmetic.
• **Zero or negative captures** — `0/0/0000` matches the slash regex but produces `'0000-00-00'`. Again, structurally valid output, semantically nonsense.
sections.why: The 'pad is mandatory not cosmetic' point is the bug-prevention argument — most candidates think `padStart` is for display formatting, but here it's load-bearing for dedupe and sort to work. Calling out the false-positive ceiling (~95%) is the senior-tier signal: it shows you've shipped scanners and you know NLP-free regex maxes out at high-90s for messy real-world text. Promising 100% is a red flag.

sections.title: 5. Complexity & memory
sections.prompt: How would you defend the bounds?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n + k) where n is the length of the input text and k is the number of matches. The three `matchAll` calls each scan the text once — that's 3n work — and each match does O(1) normalization (small string ops, table lookup). The final `.sort()` is O(k log k) on the unique-count k.

Space is O(k) for the Set, plus the O(k) sorted array at the end. The text itself is read-only; we don't allocate a copy.

If this were called on very long texts repeatedly, the regex objects should be hoisted out of the function so they're compiled once. JavaScript's regex engine caches literals in modern V8, but in a hot path I'd lift them to module-level constants to be explicit.

The interesting tradeoff: we do three passes over the same string instead of one. A single mega-regex with three alternatives would be one pass but much harder to read and maintain. For text-extraction code, readability of regex >> the constant-factor savings."
sections.why: The three-passes vs. mega-regex tradeoff is the senior-tier call — most candidates either don't notice or default to the mega-regex because 'one pass is faster'. Defending the three-pass version on maintenance grounds shows you've maintained regex code and know that the next person reading it will thank you. The 'hoist regex literals out of hot paths' note is a real production concern that most candidates skip.

sections.title: 6. Robustness & tests
sections.prompt: What would you write to lock this in?
sections.say:
"Test cases I'd want before shipping:"

• **Single date in each format** — ISO, slash, long-month-full (`January`), long-month-abbrev (`Jan`). Four trivial cases that confirm each branch fires.
• **Same date in two formats** — assert dedupe collapses to one entry. The Set test.
• **Multiple dates across formats** — confirms the sort returns chronological order. The ISO-sort-equals-chronological-sort claim under test.
• **Period after abbreviation** — `Jan. 5, 2024` should still match (the `\.?` in the regex).
• **Unknown month word** — `Foo 5, 2024` should produce zero matches, not crash. The `if (mo)` guard test.
• **Embedded structural false positive** — `pages 1/2/2024` matches; locked-down behavior to be aware of, not necessarily 'fixed'.
• **Empty string** — returns `[]`.
• **All-whitespace string** — returns `[]`.

"Beyond tests: if this were the date-extraction layer of a real legal-tech product, I'd pair it with a confidence score per match (regex precision is high but not perfect) and let the UI surface low-confidence dates for human review. The extractor is the kernel; confidence + review is the production wrapper."
sections.why: The unknown-month test is the highest-value coverage — it locks down the `if (mo)` guard against silent regressions where someone 'simplifies' the lookup. The confidence-score extension at the end is the production-tier signal: it shows you see regex extraction as a probabilistic process that needs a human-in-the-loop, not a parse-everything-perfectly function. That's how this code would actually deploy.

walkthrough.intro: Step through extractDates on a short medical note. The trace yields once per regex match and once when the dedupe Set short-circuits a re-add, so you can watch the canonical ISO strings accumulate and collapse.

examples.label: Mixed-format note → 3 dedupe'd dates
examples.input: Initial visit Jan 5, 2024. Follow-up 02/10/2024. MRI on 2024-01-05 confirmed. Discharged March 3, 2024.

trace: const months = { january:1, february:2, march:3, april:4, may:5, june:6, july:7, august:8, september:9, october:10, november:11, december:12, jan:1, feb:2, mar:3, apr:4, jun:6, jul:7, aug:8, sep:9, sept:9, oct:10, nov:11, dec:12 };
yield { line: 1, label: `enter extractDates — text.length=${text.length}, found={}`, state: { textPreview: text.slice(0, 60) + (text.length > 60 ? '…' : ''), found: [] } };
yield { line: 5, label: `pass 1: ISO /\\b(\\d{4})-(\\d{2})-(\\d{2})\\b/g`, state: { pass: 'ISO', found: [...found] } };
yield { line: 6, label: `ISO match '${m[0]}' → '${iso}'${had ? ' (already in Set — dedupe)' : ' → add'}`, state: { match: m[0], iso, had, found: [...found] } };
yield { line: 8, label: `pass 2: US-slash /\\b(\\d{1,2})/(\\d{1,2})/(\\d{4})\\b/g`, state: { pass: 'slash', found: [...found] } };
yield { line: 9, label: `slash match '${m[0]}' → MM=${m[1]}, DD=${m[2]}, YYYY=${m[3]} → '${iso}'${had ? ' (dedupe)' : ' → add'}`, state: { match: m[0], iso, had, found: [...found] } };
yield { line: 11, label: `pass 3: long-month /\\b([A-Za-z]+)\\.?\\s+(\\d{1,2}),\\s+(\\d{4})\\b/g`, state: { pass: 'long-month', found: [...found] } };

yield { line: 13, label: `long-month match '${m[0]}' → month='${m[1]}'→${mo}, day=${m[2]}, year=${m[3]} → '${iso}'${had ? ' (dedupe)' : ' → add'}`, state: { match: m[0], iso, had, found: [...found] } };
yield { line: 13, label: `long-month '${m[0]}' — months['${m[1].toLowerCase()}'] is undefined → skip`, state: { match: m[0], found: [...found] } };
yield { line: 16, label: `[...found].sort() — ISO strings sort chronologically → ${JSON.stringify(sorted)}`, state: { found: [...found], sorted, returns: JSON.stringify(sorted) } };

notes: Normalizing every format to ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` and storing in a `Set` makes 'Jan 5, 2024' and '2024-01-05' dedupe automatically — they collapse to the same canonical string.
ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` is designed so lexicographic (plain string) sort equals chronological order; no Date parsing or custom comparator needed.
`matchAll` with the `/g` flag returns every match as an iterable of arrays where `m[1]`, `m[2]`, `m[3]` are the capture groups — unlike `match` with `/g`, which drops the groups.
Time O(n + k log k), Space O(k) — three linear passes over text length n; k unique dates collected into a Set, then sorted (k ≤ total matches ≤ n).

questions.q: Why store normalized ISO strings in a `Set` rather than pushing to an array?
options: A Set returns its elements in sorted order, so `.sort()` becomes a no-op
The same calendar date written in two formats ('Jan 5, 2024' and '2024-01-05') normalizes to the same string, and the Set dedupes them automatically
Arrays would push the regex `Match` objects whole; Set unwraps them to strings
Set guarantees `O(1)` `.has()` while array `.includes()` is `O(n)`, so the regex passes run faster
questions.explain: Both formats map to the canonical '2024-01-05'. Adding both to a Set keeps just one copy, so the multi-format extraction doesn't report the same date twice.

questions.q: Why does `[...found].sort()` (a plain string sort) produce chronological order?
options: `Array.prototype.sort` checks for `Date.parse`-able strings and routes through numeric comparison
ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` is fixed-width with the most-significant field (year) first, so lexicographic string order equals chronological order
The hyphen is treated as a digit-zero in lexicographic comparison, so year and month align
Spread iteration over a Set yields entries in insertion order, which here matches chronological order
questions.explain: Year-month-day ordering with zero-padding means comparing the strings character-by-character compares year, then month, then day — exactly chronological. No Date objects or comparators required.

options: `match` advances `lastIndex` between calls, so re-running it on the same text would skip matches
matchAll yields each match WITH its capture groups (m[1], m[2], m[3]); match with /g returns just the full matched strings and discards the groups
`match` requires the regex to be wrapped in `new RegExp(...)`; `matchAll` accepts the literal directly
`matchAll` returns a lazy iterator so we can `break` after the first match if needed
questions.explain: The code needs the year/month/day capture groups to reassemble each date. `String.match` with `/g` throws the groups away and returns only full-match strings, so `matchAll` is required to get the parts.

questions.q: For the US-slash format, why is the group order `${m[3]}-${pad(+m[1])}-${pad(+m[2])}`?
options: The matchAll iterator emits groups in regex-right-to-left order, so m[3] is the leftmost capture
The input is MM/DD/YYYY, so group 1 is month, group 2 is day, group 3 is year — reordered and zero-padded to YYYY-MM-DD
Capture group 3 is always the year by convention in JS regex literals
The `+` coercion swaps m[1] and m[3] so the year ends up first
questions.explain: `02/10/2024` is MM/DD/YYYY: m[1]='02' (month), m[2]='10' (day), m[3]='2024' (year). Emitting year-month-day with `pad` produces the ISO '2024-02-10'. The `+` coerces to number so `pad` re-pads consistently.

L3.prompt: Extract every date from a medical note in three formats — `2024-01-05`, `01/05/2024` (MM/DD/YYYY), and `Jan 5, 2024` / `January 5, 2024` — normalize each to ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`, dedupe, and return sorted ascending.
hints: Run three `matchAll` passes — one per format — and `found.add(...)` a normalized ISO string from each.
Use a Set so a date written two ways ('Jan 5, 2024' and '2024-01-05') dedupes to one entry. Zero-pad month/day with `String(n).padStart(2, '0')`.
Return `[...found].sort()` — ISO strings sort chronologically with a plain string sort, no comparator needed.
